Clarity.justification: The paper is exceptionally well-structured with logical sections (Abstract, Introduction, Related Work, Method, Experimental Setup, Results, Discussion, Conclusion). Ideas are clearly articulated using precise terminology, tables (e.g., oracle isolation metrics, adaptive PBT results), and figures (e.g., gate metrics bar charts, failure rate scatter plots, violin distributions). Statistical reporting includes 95% CIs, Wilcoxon p-values, Spearman/Kendall coefficients, and bootstrap details. Minor issues include absolute figure paths in the text and occasional dense notation, but overall coherence and readability are high.

Novelty.justification: The core contribution—the oracle isolation design using ContractEval's CVT inputs to decouple oracle semantics from input generation—is original. It quantifies a 0.40 oracle-isolation gap (with 0.40 contract-unique mass) across 364 tasks and multiple LLMs, and demonstrates an independent ~0.10 adaptive PBT contribution. Principled negative results (Spearman ρ=0.136, negligible cross-model ΔR²=0.004) are informative. This advances LLM code evaluation beyond dense differential testing (EvalPlus) by integrating formal contracts, though it builds incrementally on ContractEval and property-based testing literature.

Soundness.justification: Methods are appropriate and rigorously implemented: CVT inputs enable controlled oracle comparison; statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank with Holm correction, exact permutation tests, MixedLM, bootstrap CIs) are correctly applied with reported p-values and convergence details. Code artifacts (multiprocessing pools, SIGALRM timeouts, Hypothesis PBT, AST richness scoring) demonstrate reproducibility. Results are consistent across 5 model families (10,432–17,226 triples) and task types. Limitations (CVT scope, n=5 models for ranking) are explicitly acknowledged. Experimental outputs (JSONL results, per-task CSVs) align with reported metrics and figures.

Significance.justification: The work addresses a critical gap in LLM code evaluation: dense test suites (764 tests/task) miss 40% of contract violations on contract-relevant inputs. It provides empirical evidence for oracle-type diversity as a first-class dimension and supplies a reproducible methodology (CVT-based isolation) applicable to any contract-annotated benchmark. Impact is high for verification communities and benchmarks (EvalPlus, ContractEval), though generalization is scoped to Python algorithmic tasks and execution-based oracles.

strengths: Rigorous oracle-isolation design with controlled CVT inputs yielding a clear, statistically significant 0.40 gap
Comprehensive experiments across 364 tasks, 5 LLMs, and two orthogonal experiments (isolation + adaptive PBT) with principled negative results
weaknesses: Cross-model ranking analysis is underpowered (n=5 models) and reports structural p-value limitations
All claims scoped to CVT inputs and Python algorithmic tasks; broader generalization (random inputs, other languages) remains open
